summary: A proposal that an FTP server should allow a limited kind of access without a user name and password, since people were using the mail file facility as a workaround for files they could not otherwise fetch. It suggests a new class of everyone, whether or not logged on. Later notes such as RFC 501 criticized the details.

eli5.summary: People kept finding sneaky ways to get public files because the front desk demanded a password. This asks for a public window anyone can use.

subtitle: A 1973 proposal that FTP servers let anyone fetch publicly marked files without a user name and password.

tldr.problem: FTP servers on systems with security demanded a user name and password, so people with no account on a system could not transfer files and fell back on the MAIL FILE facility.
tldr.mechanism: If a user makes a file request without a name and password, the server should check the file's access parameters and let the transfer proceed when the file is listed as accessible to anyone.
tldr.outcome: BBN TENEX agreed to try it, and the author urged other systems to offer it experimentally. RFC 501 later criticized the proposal's assumptions.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 487 as Unknown, and it is not marked as obsoleted or updated. RFC 501 responds to it with objections.

sections.title: The Problem with Passwords
sections.content:
Bob Bressler of BBN reports that many people had trouble transferring files. The trouble was with systems that have some flavor of security but on which the user has no access privileges. The FTP server demanded a user name and password before it granted any system access.

The workaround people used was the MAIL FILE facility, which the RFC calls both limited in scope and intended for other purposes.
sections.eli5: Imagine a library that makes you show a card even to read a poster on the wall. People started slipping posters through the mail slot instead.

sections.title: The Proposal
sections.content:
A common file protection model has three levels: only the user, all users in a group, or everyone. Until then, everyone had meant anyone already allowed to log on. The RFC suggests a new class that covers everyone, whether or not they are logged on.

Under the proposal, a user who connects to an FTP server and makes a file request without a name and password causes the server to examine the file access parameters. If the file is accessible to anyone, the transfer should be allowed to proceed.

The scheme need not give file creation privileges. Store commands could work through an append mechanism: to receive a file, a person creates an empty file with unlimited append access and tells the sender to store to it.
sections.eli5: Files get a new label, open to everybody. If a file has that label, the server hands it over without asking for a password.

sections.title: Accounting and Rollout
sections.content:
The RFC notes that accounting is more complex. Storing a file in a user's directory can be charged to that user, covering CPU time and secondary storage. Retrieving a file from a general system directory has no user to charge, so overhead may have to be billed, but only CPU charges are involved and they may be small.

BBN TENEX agreed to modify its FTP server. A note adds that the TENEX implementation will probably require a user name such as FREE or ANONYMOUS but no password. The author urged other systems to offer the service, if only experimentally, and said success would be judged by the reaction of users and the uses made of FTP.
sections.eli5: Someone has to pay for the electricity when guests borrow files. The author thinks the cost is small and wants to try it and see.

references.text: Pogran, K., "Un-Muddling Free File Transfer", RFC 501, May 1973 (a later response, not cited by this RFC).
